statements.quote: The authors used a large language model (Claude, Anthropic) to assist with language editing, refining the logical flow of arguments, and drafting analysis and visualization code. The study design, data collection, analyses, and results are entirely the authors’ work. The authors reviewed, verified, and edited all text and take full responsibility for the content of the manuscript.
statements.locator: p. 1, Author notes

statements.quote: We tested both challenges in a preregistered creative metaphor experiment with native (L1) and non-native (L2) English writers, who wrote without AI, with AI-generated ideas (AI ideation), or with AI refining their own ideas (AI refinement).
statements.locator: p. 2, Abstract

statements.quote: The human experiment, including the three conditions and the L1/L2 comparison, was preregistered (link: https://tinyurl.com/DiverseCreativity).
statements.locator: p. 4, Introduction, experimental-design paragraph

statements.quote: Finally, going beyond the preregistered design, we compared these human pools against LLM-simulated answers generated from personas built on the real participants’ background information.
statements.locator: p. 5, Introduction, experimental-design paragraph

statements.quote: We report the key findings in the text; full model specifications and coefficients are in SI Appendix, Tables S1-S3.
statements.locator: p. 6, Results, opening paragraph

statements.quote: As preregistered, we first examined how AI assistance reshapes the collective diversity of human metaphor pools (Fig. 2A).
statements.locator: p. 6, Results, Human linguistic diversity fuels collective diversity

statements.quote: This language-choice comparison was preregistered as exploratory, and we interpret it accordingly.
statements.locator: p. 8, Results, native-language comparison

statements.quote: When we instead embedded metaphors together with their explanations (SI Appendix, Fig. S1), the refinement pools also drifted toward the centroid relative to the human-only baseline (AI ideation: b = 0.028, p = 0.019; AI refinement: b = 0.046, p < 0.001), and the two AI conditions did not differ (b = 0.018, p = 0.12).
statements.locator: p. 8, Results, supplementary metaphor-plus-explanation analysis

statements.quote: For every participant in all three human conditions, we built a persona from their background information (including age, sex, ethnicity, education level, first language, etc.; see Fig. S2 for a sample prompt) and asked three model families (GPT-4o mini, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Qwen3.5-27b) to complete the same set of metaphor tasks.
statements.locator: p. 9, Results, LLM-simulated diversity

statements.quote: These simulation analyses were not preregistered; we treat them as an adversarial extension and stacked every analytic choice in the simulation’s favor.
statements.locator: p. 9, Results, LLM-simulated diversity

statements.quote: This raised simulated diversity across all three models (Fig. 3B; see Fig. S3 for subgroup distributions), most visibly for the weakest model (GPT-4o mini including L2 persona with native languages vs. only with English output: M = 0.606 vs. 0.698, Δ = -0.092, p < 0.001), mirroring the human native-language effect in direction.
statements.locator: p. 10, Results, reference to SI Fig. S3

statements.quote: Quantile regressions (SI Appendix, Fig. S4) show that AI ideation raised convergent creativity across the rating distribution for both groups, whereas its divergent effect was concentrated in the bottom quantiles for L1 writers (β = +7.5, p < 0.001 at τ = 0.1 vs. β = +4.5, p = 0.003 at τ = 0.9) and existed only there for L2 writers (significant only at τ ≤ 0.2).
statements.locator: p. 13, Results, reference to SI Fig. S4

statements.quote: We preregistered a target of 600 writers, 100 per cell in the 2 × 3 design, and ultimately recruited 644 writers via Prolific between March 11 and 15, 2026.
statements.locator: p. 16, Materials and Methods, Participants, Writers

statements.quote: All participants provided informed consent and were informed that their anonymized research data could be shared for research purposes. All data, materials, and analysis code are openly available at https://osf.io/amgx9/overview?view_only=46c491afd0ba40fc91f361aa2b53be79.
statements.locator: p. 17, Materials and Methods, Ethics

statements.quote: Within the two AI conditions, L2 writers additionally chose their language for AI interaction (English vs. native language), a comparison preregistered as exploratory.
statements.locator: p. 17, Materials and Methods, Writing task and materials

statements.quote: All writers responded to the same four scenarios, presented in a randomized order: (1) “Think of the most boring high-school or college class you've ever had. What was it like to sit through?”; (2) “Think about the most disgusting thing you ever ate or drank. What was it like to eat or drink it?”; (3) “Think about the worst movie or TV show you have ever seen. What was it like to watch it?”; and (4) “Think of the messiest room that you've ever had to live in. What was it like to live there?”. For each scenario, writers produced one creative metaphor in a fixed two-part format, “It feels like ___. This is because ___”, comprising a metaphor and a short explanation. Instructions emphasized producing novel, surprising comparisons and avoiding clichés.
statements.locator: p. 17, Materials and Methods, Writing task and materials

statements.quote: To deter covert AI use, the survey embedded JavaScript checks that detected tab or window switching: the first switch triggered a warning, and a second switch terminated the session.
statements.locator: p. 17, Materials and Methods, Human-only condition, JavaScript checks

statements.quote: Before composing each metaphor, writers received five AI-generated candidate metaphors, each with a short explanation, generated by GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06) with the system message reproduced in SI Appendix, Figs. S5 and S6.
statements.locator: p. 17, Materials and Methods, AI ideation condition

statements.quote: They then received five AI-generated candidate explanations for their metaphor, generated by GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06) with the system message in SI Appendix, Figs. S7 and S8, and finalized their explanation, again free to adopt, adapt, or ignore the suggestions.
statements.locator: pp. 17-18, Materials and Methods, AI refinement condition

statements.quote: Evaluators rated each metaphor together with its explanation on four items, each on a 0-100 slider (0 = not at all to 100 = extremely). Evaluators were blind to the writers’ background and condition, and no information about AI involvement was provided. To counter scale compression, instructions asked evaluators to use the full range and to assign roughly as many ratings below 50 as above 50. The four items were specified as below: (1) Novelty: How novel or original is this metaphor? A novel metaphor is unexpected and avoids familiar or clichéd comparisons; (2) Surprise: How surprising is this metaphor? Does it catch you off guard in a meaningful way? (3) Appropriateness: How appropriate or fitting is this metaphor? Does the comparison make sense for the scenario described? (4) Explanation quality: How well does the explanation capture why the metaphor works? Does it help you understand the connection between metaphor and experience? Novelty and surprise were averaged into a divergent-creativity subscale (Spearman-Brown rSB = 0.86), and appropriateness and explanation aptness into a convergent-creativity subscale (Spearman-Brown rSB = 0.87), following the standard distinction between the originality and the appropriateness components of creativity (Doshi & Hauser, 2024; Lee & Chung, 2024; Runco & Jaeger, 2012; Silvia & Beaty, 2012).
statements.locator: p. 18, Materials and Methods, Evaluation task (rating materials)

statements.quote: For every writer in all three conditions, we constructed a persona prompt from their background questionnaire: age, gender, ethnicity, native language, education, household income, subjective social status (0-10 ladder), political orientation, and AI use and literacy (sample prompt in SI Appendix, Fig. S2).
statements.locator: p. 19, Materials and Methods, LLM simulation of the writer pool

statements.quote: These simulation analyses were not preregistered; all design choices were made to favor the simulation.
statements.locator: p. 19, Materials and Methods, LLM simulation of the writer pool

statements.quote: The experiment, including the three writing conditions, the L1/L2 comparison, and the collective and individual outcome families, was preregistered (link at https://tinyurl.com/DiverseCreativity). The language-choice comparison among L2 writers was preregistered as exploratory. The LLM simulations and the quantile-regression analyses were not preregistered and are reported as exploratory extensions.
statements.locator: p. 20, Preregistration and deviations, first paragraph

statements.quote: The preregistration specified multiple measures for both collective- and individual-level outcome families. Two analytic choices were made after registration, which we note for transparency. First, among the preregistered collective-diversity measures (centroid similarity, semantic distance, and lexical diversity), we report centroid similarity as the primary measure, for comparability with prior work (Doshi & Hauser, 2024). The other preregistered measures are also reported in the SI Appendix, Fig. S9. Second, among the preregistered measures of individual creative performance, we rely on blinded human ratings rather than automated LLM-based scoring. In validation, the LLM scorers produced inconsistent rankings across scoring models and systematically favored LLM-generated content, a circularity that would bias precisely the comparisons this study is about (details in SI Appendix, Fig. S10).
statements.locator: p. 20, Preregistration and deviations, second paragraph

statements.quote: Fig. S2. Example simulation prompt, constructed for a persona of an L1 participant. The system message concatenates the participant's real background (age, gender, ethnicity, native language, education, household income, social-ladder standing, political orientation, and AI use and literacy) with the task instruction; the user message supplies one of the four scenarios.

deposits.notes:
Checked 2026-10-09. The paper URL and the identical form data_url/code_url returned HTTP 200. OSF identifies project amgx9 as 'Diverse creativity', public=false, but its published view-only link permits anonymous metadata, file listing, and downloads without an account. 'public' here means accessible through that published link.

API checks: https://api.osf.io/v2/nodes/amgx9/?view_only=46c491afd0ba40fc91f361aa2b53be79 returned 200; https://api.osf.io/v2/nodes/amgx9/files/osfstorage/?view_only=46c491afd0ba40fc91f361aa2b53be79 returned 200; https://api.osf.io/v2/nodes/amgx9/children/?view_only=46c491afd0ba40fc91f361aa2b53be79 returned 200 with zero children. The providers endpoint returned 200 with only osfstorage. All 24 nested folder listings returned 200, and pagination was exhausted. There are 67 regular files: 34 data files, 18 scripts, 11 figures, and 4 root files. The 50 listed files comprise all 34 data files, 15 analysis/support scripts, and README.md; omitted from this capped list are 11 figure PNGs, 3 root configuration files, and 3 LLM-scoring generation scripts.

rows_checked and columns_checked refer to data/writing/intermediate/metaphors_with_metrics.csv (HTTP 200; 1,169,844 bytes). It contains 2,493 unique PID-by-scenario records from 644 unique writers, with no writer assigned to multiple base arms. Observed analyzed-writer counts after collapsing condition suffixes: NO_AI=204, IDEATION=238, REFINEMENT=202 (440 across both AI arms). L1 counts are 106, 110, 102 respectively; L2 counts are 98, 128, 100 respectively. These are counts computed from the downloaded data, not randomized counts from the PDF. Eighteen writers have 1 retained metaphor, 12 have 2, 5 have 3, and 609 have 4, accounting for the 83-output shortfall relative to four outputs per 644 writers; the cause of the omissions is not established by these files.

All 2,493 records have condition, metaphor, reason, semantic_distance, semantic_distance_full, ttr_metaphor, and ttr_full populated. condition has NO_AI, IDEATION, REFINEMENT, IDEATION_EN, IDEATION_Non-EN, REFINEMENT_EN, and REFINEMENT_Non-EN. PID is a writer pseudonym; RID is a response pseudonym. has_arm_assignment=true denotes a recorded arm, not confirmation of random allocation. has_outcome_scores=true refers to automated scores and LLM-judge scores, not individual human ratings.

Also downloaded and parsed in memory (all HTTP 200): metaphors_long.csv, 2,493 rows and 644 unique PIDs, with PID, RID, condition, group, scenario_num, scenario_name, scenario_text, metaphor, reason, timer_page_submit, timer_first_click, timer_click_count; l2_language_data.csv, 344 rows, with PID, native_language, ai_language_self_report, user_lang_detail; raw/L1.csv, 339 CSV records, and raw/L2.csv, 366 CSV records, containing RID and reduced demographic/AI-literacy fields. These last two record counts are not claimed as analyzed participant counts.

metaphor_embeddings.npy and full_text_embeddings.npy were both downloaded into memory (HTTP 200; 3,829,376 bytes each) and read with numpy, allow_pickle=false: each has shape (2493, 384), dtype float32, finite values, and unit-normalized rows. The CSV's embedding_idx links outputs to the stored embeddings. The posted scripts recompute centroid similarity and mean pairwise cosine distance from these embeddings, so diversity outcomes do not require new model calls.

IMPORTANT INCOMPLETENESS: README.md says that data/evaluation/intermediate/ratings_long.csv is shipped, but it is absent from the complete recursive listing. data/evaluation contains only four aggregate CSVs under output/: mixed_regression.csv, model_summaries.csv, reliability.csv, and quantile_stats.csv. The README explicitly excludes raw/evaluation survey.csv and metaphor_long_format.csv; neither is present. Evaluation scripts and LLM validation code require the missing ratings_long.csv. No individual human novelty, surprise, appropriateness, or explanation-quality ratings were found. Therefore S1-O6/S1-O7 per-writer means, SDs, SEs, whole-sample rating contrasts, and the rating-specific counts cannot be reconstructed from this deposit as inspected.

All three per-judge creativity-score CSVs were parsed (HTTP 200): gpt4o_creativity_scores.csv, claude_sonnet_creativity_scores.csv, qwen3_creativity_scores.csv. Each has 2,532 rows, 650 unique PIDs, and 2,524 unique PID-by-scenario keys, including every one of the 2,493 retained writing keys plus 31 other keys. These files require sample restriction and duplicate-key resolution before analysis. Shared columns include PID, RID, condition, group, scenario_name, metaphor, reason, semantic_distance, semantic_distance_full, and ttr_full; GPT/Claude score columns include bt_raw_metaphor, pct_metaphor, z_metaphor, bt_raw_full, pct_full, z_full; Qwen uses these names with _vllm suffixes. llm_judge_scores.csv has 2,483 rows and columns scenario_name, metaphor, condition, group, GPT-4o mini, Claude Sonnet 4, Qwen3-8B; it has no PID and no human score column. The paper's human-versus-LLM validation subset cannot be recovered without the missing human ratings.

Additional readable aggregate outputs: data/evaluation/output/mixed_regression.csv (28 coefficient rows) and data/writing/output/mixed_regression.csv (28 coefficient rows) have analysis, outcome, term, beta, SE, z, p, sig, ci_lo, ci_hi; both include simple effects at L2 that the PDF omits or confuses with interactions. data/evaluation/output/model_summaries.csv has 4 model rows. These are model summaries, not a replacement for participant-level human ratings.

S2 is also represented: data/simulation/intermediate/clean_participants.csv has 609 rows and columns RID, PID, group, CONDITION, base_cond; clean_metaphors_long.csv has 2,436 rows from those 609 PIDs. data/simulation/output/english/anthropic.csv was parsed (HTTP 200; 2,436 rows, 609 unique PIDs), with PID, group, condition_origin, native_language, scenario_name, scenario_text, model, provider, temperature, metaphor, reason, parse_ok, raw_response, gen_language, translated, translate_model, native_metaphor, native_reason, english_metaphor. Other English, native-language, and temperature-sweep model files were listed but not all downloaded. The simulation sample of 609 differs from the 644-writer writing sample and must not be conflated with it.

Code was read as text, not executed. scripts/writing/02_omnibus_models.py computes the main model outcome within scenario x base condition, pooling L1 and L2; its AI-language model uses scenario x condition x language-group pools. scripts/writing/01_collective_diversity.py separately uses background-specific and language-specific centroids for plotted subgroup results, while also computing whole-condition pools. scripts/writing/03_alt_diversity_measures.py defines mean pairwise cosine distance per metaphor within scenario x condition x writer background and reads semantic_distance and ttr_metaphor as per-output columns. The exact preparation code for those precomputed semantic-distance/TTR columns is not included among the listed writing scripts.

No data/code license was found in the node metadata, README, or file inventory, so license is null. The separate preregistration's CC BY 4.0 license is not assumed to cover this deposit. The posting contains analysis/generation code, but no study-allocation implementation or original writer-survey export sufficient to settle random assignment or the disputed L2 refinement prompt. README says raw non-English message samples and other identifying/free-response survey fields were removed, while the de-identified English metaphor and explanation texts are retained.

The paper's https://tinyurl.com/DiverseCreativity returned HTTP 200 after redirecting to this OSF view-only URL. The registration title is 'Diverse Creativity Using Generative AI: Writing Task'. what_we_could_compute: Writers per arm (open question 2): count unique PID in the retained writing data by condition, including L1/L2 and language subgroups. The confirmed counts are 204 No AI, 238 AI ideation, and 202 AI refinement; 440 writers are in the AI arms for diversity analyses. The missing rating data prevent checking the corresponding 441-writer rating-model sample.

Whole-sample diversity effects and participant-level dispersion (open questions 5 and 10): compute each writer's mean across available metaphors, then arm means, SDs, SEs and standardized contrasts for S1-O1 through S1-O5. Texts, explanations, embeddings, precomputed semantic-distance/TTR values, participant IDs, and arms are available. Whole-arm and background-specific centroid or pairwise diversity measures can be computed using explicit pooling choices; diversity-model uncertainty can be obtained by refitting the posted analysis.

Centroid pooling and the alternative-measure unit (open questions 7 and 8, plus the unresolved S1-O3 item): inspect the code to distinguish whole-condition centroids in the main mixed model from subgroup centroids in figures, verify that mean pairwise distance is per metaphor, and identify per-metaphor semantic-distance/TTR columns. The code and data support recomputing the diversity statistics rather than extracting figure-only values.

Missing-output accounting (open question 3): count retained metaphors per writer and scenario to account arithmetically for the 2,493 versus 2,576 outputs. The files do not establish why particular outputs are absent or whether the tab-switch terminations are inside the reported sample.

L2 refinement simple effects and model SEs (open questions 6 and 10): recover the already-exported coefficient and SE rows from data/evaluation/output/mixed_regression.csv and data/writing/output/mixed_regression.csv. These exports do not supply participant-level human-rating SDs or permit arbitrary new rating contrasts.

LLM-judge outcome S1-O8: participant-linked score files permit writer/arm summaries after restricting to the analyzed writing sample and resolving duplicate PID-by-scenario keys. The unavailable human-rating data prevent reconstructing the paper's human-versus-LLM comparison subset and its human correlations.
notes:
Public participant-linked texts and automated outcome data are confirmed, but overall status is public_partial because the key individual human-rating data for S1-O6/S1-O7 are absent despite the README claiming they are shipped. No participant-level human-rating means, SDs, SEs, pooled rating effects, or rating-specific sample discrepancies can be resolved from the inspected deposit. has_outcome_scores=true is limited to the automated/LLM outcomes; it does not indicate that every outcome is available.

The complete markdown conversion was read, including the SI Appendix on PDF pp. 23-29. Statements were checked against pymupdf text from the 29-page PDF identified in retrieval.json. Quotes preserve wording and punctuation, with line/page-wrap whitespace normalized and split hyphenated words rejoined. No extra data/code repository URL was found in the appendix; the only two unique external availability/preregistration links are the OSF project and the TinyURL preregistration.

The source is an arXiv preprint, with no journal publisher or journal supplement identified. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26899 returned HTTP 200 and lists version 1; its landing-page links contained no separate paper-specific supplementary dataset. The SI Appendix is inside the saved PDF. Exact-title and first-author searches at DataCite, Zenodo, Harvard Dataverse, and OSF, plus the author's public OSF projects, found no additional relevant data deposit.

Availability was checked on 2026-10-09 with Python urllib using User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1 and no personal identifier. No login, account creation, access request, or bot-check bypass was used. Downloaded data and code were read in memory; every downloaded data file was below 20 MB. Only the requested forms/data/c054.json output was written. S1 random assignment remains unconfirmed; the availability findings do not change that screening conclusion.
